blocks.en: Abstract
blocks.zh: 摘要

blocks.en: Large language models are increasingly used as judges to reduce reliance on costly human evaluation, yet their scores can systematically disagree with human judgments. We ask whether responses to an explicitly imposed evaluative bias can help correct a judge's implicit scoring biases. We introduce PRISM (Probe-based Residual Inference of Scoring Misalignment), which holds the evaluated content fixed and measures score changes when attributes are emphasized or de-emphasized. A local sensitivity model motivates representing these responses as a surrogate Jacobian. Ridge regression on human labels learns a correction to the baseline score. The resulting scoring protocol is rubric-free: it uses overall scores without requesting criterion-level ratings. In the main Jev and Sol comparisons on SummEval summarization and HANNA story evaluation, PRISM and its learned-baseline variant significantly improve agreement with human rankings over uncalibrated scores while remaining competitive with rubric-based methods. A controlled SummEval comparison yields similar agreement for rubric-derived quality probes and style probes, supporting calibration without reproducing rubric criteria. The learned coefficients reveal shared and opposing correction directions across judges.

blocks.en: 1 Introduction
blocks.zh: 导言

blocks.en:
Human evaluation provides a reference for assessing generated text [ 6 ] . Large language models (LLMs) offer scalable
evaluation [ 27 ] and a source of training feedback
that reduces reliance on costly human labels [ 14 ] .
Recent releases such as Jev extend this activity to decision models
with typed probabilistic outputs for scoring and verification [ 1 , 5 ] . Yet LLM judgments can favor verbosity,
particular answer positions, or their own generations [ 27 , 25 , 22 , 18 ] . On subjective
evaluation tasks, judges can also agree with one another while
diverging from human judgments [ 17 ] .
Improving agreement with human judgments is therefore important both for
evaluation and for the feedback supplied to learning systems.

blocks.en: 1.1 Related work
blocks.zh: 1.1 相关工作

blocks.en:
Evaluator design and calibration: Specialized evaluators such as Prometheus 2 are trained for direct
assessment and pairwise ranking under user-defined criteria [ 11 ] . SAJA instead calibrates a fixed judge and
also analyzes the importance of its rubric features [ 10 ] . Recent work fits increasing affine maps to
human-rated anchors, aligning score scales while preserving rankings [ 28 ] .
Our features measure how overall scores change under shifted emphasis,
rather than the level of each criterion rating. The fitted coefficients
describe corrections in response coordinates, without identifying
the judge’s internal weights.

Bias diagnosis and correction: Position bias varies across judges and tasks [ 22 ] .
CALM diagnoses biases by modifying answers or instructions and
measuring changes in scores or preferences [ 26 ] .

from consistency under option-position and identifier swaps, without
human labels [ 12 ] . 𝙿𝚁𝙸𝚂𝙼 \mathtt{PRISM} learns a correction
from human labels and allows the probes to change the judgment;
their predictive value is tested against held-out human evaluations.

blocks.en:
Evaluation protocol: SummEval provides 100 documents with 16 summaries each. Our target
averages expert coherence, consistency, fluency, and relevance ratings.
HANNA provides 96 prompts with 11 stories each, rated by three people
on six criteria. Our main metric is Spearman correlation, also used
for LLM-judge evaluation by Liu et al. [ 13 ] and Kola et al. [ 10 ] .
We compute correlations within documents (SummEval) or prompts (HANNA)
and average across contexts to assess agreement with human rankings.
We evaluate fitted methods on the same five held-out groups of
documents or prompts,
training on the remaining groups. We choose 𝙿𝚁𝙸𝚂𝙼 \mathtt{PRISM} ’s regularization
by validation within the training data using the same metric;
exactly tied scores favor stronger regularization. Individual and
paired 95% intervals use 2,000 document/prompt-bootstrap samples.
In the main SummEval comparison, 𝙿𝚁𝙸𝚂𝙼 \mathtt{PRISM} uses single-candidate expected ratings for Jev and batched
pointwise ratings for Sol; both use single-candidate scoring on HANNA.
Full acquisition and calibration protocols, including the additional
Sonnet and Gemma settings, appear in sections A.2 and A.3 .
Model versions and inference settings are collected in section A.1 .

blocks.en: 4 Conclusion
blocks.zh: 4 结论

blocks.en:
𝙿𝚁𝙸𝚂𝙼 \mathtt{PRISM} connects perturbation analysis to rubric-free LLM evaluation.
It represents changes in overall scores under attribute-emphasis
instructions as a surrogate Jacobian and learns a ridge correction
from human labels. Inference uses only baseline and probed scores,
without requesting criterion-level judge ratings. On SummEval and
HANNA, 𝙿𝚁𝙸𝚂𝙼 \mathtt{PRISM} and α ​ - ​ 𝙿𝚁𝙸𝚂𝙼 \alpha\text{-}\mathtt{PRISM}{} significantly improve on Vanilla
in the main Jev and Sol comparisons while achieving ranking agreement
competitive with rubric-based SAJA and G-Eval. The matched
Jev–SummEval ablation yields similar agreement from rubric-derived
quality probes and style probes, supporting calibration without
reproducing rubric criteria. Learned coefficients further expose
shared and opposing correction directions across judges, making
the use of probe responses in the correction interpretable.

blocks.en: Limitations
blocks.zh: 限制

blocks.en:
We study rubric-free calibration of text-based judgments, using human
labels to fit a correction for each judge. Additional probe calls
incur inference cost, motivating comparisons under matched budgets
and adaptive probe selection. Transfer across tasks, model versions,
and rater populations remains to be tested. Benchmark contamination
cannot be ruled out; evaluation on newly collected data would
strengthen the evidence for generalization.
